This chart -- which is pro-libertarian propaganda -- does not make things more accurate or more clear. We have a political spectrum, tried and true, that works -- if we stick to earlier definitions and don't get lost in the recent confusion of terms. It works like this:

Radical -- Liberal -- Moderate -- Conservative -- Reactionary

Or more simply:

Liberal -- Conservative

We can talk about economic or social categories, if people insist upon quadrants. What we don't need is an axis of authoritarian-libertarian which pulls out known traditional understandings of liberal and conservative, elevates libertarianism to a whole new scale, and compares it to something virtually no one can support, namely authoritarianism -- which, of course, makes libertarianism look good. If that's not libertarian propaganda, it would be hard to find anything that is.

Libertarianism is a dot (or multiple dots) on the scale of liberal versus conservative. We can debate where on the scale it is -- but we should not just go and make it its own thing.

Think of liberal and conservative as concepts. Analysis is difficult at times. It can only be simplified so much.

Take two positions on an issue. Then, ask yourself which of these two positions represents the first definition at dictionary.com for the concept words. One position will be closer to liberal, one will be closer to conservative. Usually, it is easy to decide which is which but there are some major exceptions -- gun rights and immigration probably chief among them.

When it comes to defining a platform or even an person as liberal or conservative, just about nobody is going to fit neatly into one category. As concepts, one can only be relatively liberal or conservative and it may be hard to tell.

But to complicate the concepts by elevating libertarianism to its own thing will not help anyone understand.

What is libertarianism basically? It is often described as a platform of social liberalism and economic conservatism. While I strongly disagree with this understanding, let's just say its true for the sake of the discussion.

Then, it follows naturally that a four-category classification system should include the roots of libertarianism as its y-axis and place libertarians as a dot on the graph. This is root analysis that simplifies the spectrum. Now, we can begin to work on the harder questions of where on the scale a particular platform or issue would be.

Bottom line: complicating the simple political spectrum to attempt to simplify the analysis actually distorts the analysis and produces bad results.
